metadata.title: An improved incidence bound for fields of prime order

extraction_notes.note: The proof of Theorem 3 is a whole section split over five subsections with no proof environment; per the continued-proof rule each subsection part is its own proof node proving TP3, each continuation pointing a uses edge at PP2.
The starred 'Interpretation' environment is an informal reading of Rudnev's lemma ('few' undefined), so it is a remark with heuristic rigor rather than a claim.
Claim or exercise: the extension to F_q is asserted and 'left as an exercise for the motivated reader'; kept as a semi-formal claim.
Origin paper or external: described as a straightforward modification of a Bourgain-Garaev lemma and proved in the appendix; kept as paper.
Results only mentioned without statement (Toth over C, Solymosi-Tao, the author's F_q extension [me1], Vinh) get no nodes.
The proof sketch is taken from 'The proof of Theorem 3 begins' to the contradiction, excluding the preceding Rudnev lemma and interpretation, which are separate nodes.

nodes.name: Asymptotic notation $\ll$, $O$, $\Omega$
nodes.statement: If $f$ and $g$ are functions and there is a constant $C$ such that $f(x)\leq C g(x)$ for all $x$ then we will write $f\ll g$, $f=O(g)$, or $g=\Omega(f)$.
nodes.statement_short: $f\ll g$ means $f\le Cg$ for an absolute constant $C$.

nodes.name: Logarithmic-loss notation $\lesssim$, $\widetilde{O}$, $\widetilde{\Omega}$
nodes.statement: If there is a constant $c$ such that $f \ll g \log^c x$ then we will write $f \lesssim g$, $f=\widetilde{O}(g)$ or $g=\widetilde{\Omega}(f)$.
nodes.statement_short: $f\lesssim g$ means $f\ll g$ up to a power of $\log x$.

nodes.name: Notation $\approx$
nodes.statement: If $f(x) \lesssim g(x)$ and $g(x) \lesssim f(x)$ then we will write $f(x) \approx g(x)$.

nodes.name: Parameter-dependent implicit constants
nodes.statement: The implicit constants $C$ and $c$ may vary with different instances of the notation. If one or other of them depends on a parameter $\epsilon$ then this will be indicated by a subscript, e.g. $f=O_{\epsilon}(g)$ etc.
nodes.statement_short: Implicit constants may vary; dependence on a parameter is shown by a subscript.

nodes.name: Sumset
nodes.statement: If $A$ and $B$ are subsets of a field $F$, then we will write $$A+B=\left\{a+b:a \in A, b \in B\right\}.$$

nodes.name: Partial sumset along a graph $G$
nodes.statement: If $G \subseteq A \times B$ then we will write $$A\stackrel{G}{+}B=\left\{a+b:(a,b)\in G\right\}.$$ These definitions extend analogously to subtraction, multiplication and division.
nodes.statement_short: Partial sumset $A\stackrel{G}{+}B$ of sums over pairs in $G$; likewise for differences, products, ratios.

nodes.name: Incidence
nodes.statement: A point is \textit{incident} to a line if it lies on that line. Incidences are counted with multiplicity, in the sense that several lines incident to the same point determine several incidences, and vice versa.

nodes.name: Maximum number of point-line incidences
nodes.statement: We are interested in knowing the maximum number of incidences between a set $P$ of points and a set $L$ of lines, say with $|P|,|L|\leq N$.

nodes.name: Trivial incidence bound $O(N^{3/2})$
nodes.statement: But using the Cauchy-Schwartz inequality and the fact that two distinct points determine a line, it is straightforward to see that it is in fact $O(N^{3/2})$.
assumptions: using the Cauchy-Schwartz inequality and the fact that two distinct points determine a line
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz and two-points-determine-a-line give at most $O(N^{3/2})$ incidences.

nodes.name: Incidence count $I(P,L)$ and non-trivial incidence bounds
nodes.statement: So, writing $I(P,L)$ for the number of incidences between $P$ and $L$, \textit{non-trivial} incidence bounds are of the form $I(P,L)\ll N^{3/2-\epsilon}$ with $\epsilon>0$.
nodes.statement_short: $I(P,L)$ counts incidences; a non-trivial bound is $I(P,L)\ll N^{3/2-\epsilon}$ with $\epsilon>0$.

nodes.name: Optimal incidence exponent $\epsilon=1/6$
nodes.statement: A natural example shows that the best that can be hoped for is $\epsilon = 1/6$.
conclusions: the best that can be hoped for is $\epsilon = 1/6$

nodes.name: Szemerédi-Trotter theorem
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be a set of points and $L$ a set of lines in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with $|P|,|L|\leq N$. Then $I(P,L)\ll N^{4/3}=N^{\frac{3}{2}-\frac{1}{6}}$.
assumptions: $P$ be a set of points and $L$ a set of lines in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with $|P|,|L|\leq N$
nodes.label: theorem:ST

nodes.name: Helfgott-Rudnev incidence theorem
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbb{F}_p$ be the finite field of prime order $p$. Let $P$ be a set of points and $L$ a set of lines in $\mathbb{F}_p^2$ with $|P|,|L|\leq N$ and $N<p$. Then $I(P,L)\ll N^{\frac{3}{2}-\frac{1}{10,678}}$.
assumptions: $\mathbb{F}_p$ be the finite field of prime order $p$
$P$ be a set of points and $L$ a set of lines in $\mathbb{F}_p^2$ with $|P|,|L|\leq N$ and $N<p$
nodes.label: theorem:HR

nodes.name: Bourgain-Katz-Tao incidence bound
nodes.statement: This followed work of Bourgain, Katz and Tao \cite{BKT}, which established the existence of a non-zero $\epsilon$ so long as $N<p^{2-\delta(\epsilon)}$, but did not quantify it.
nodes.statement_short: A non-trivial (unquantified) incidence exponent $\epsilon>0$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$ when $N<p^{2-\delta(\epsilon)}$.

nodes.name: Condition $N<p$ is non-degeneracy
nodes.statement: The condition $N<p$ in Theorem \ref{theorem:HR} is essentially a nondegeneracy requirement; it prevents $P$ from being the entire plane $\mathbb{F}_p^2$, in which case no nontrivial bound would be possible.

nodes.name: Erdős-Szemerédi sum-product conjecture
nodes.statement: Erd\"os and Szemer\'edi conjectured that any finite set $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ must satisfy $$\max\left\{|A+A|,|A\cdot A|\right\}\gg_{\epsilon} |A|^{2-\epsilon}$$ for any $\epsilon>0$.

nodes.name: Sum-product estimates
nodes.statement: Bounds on $\max\left\{|A+A|,|A\cdot A|\right\}$ are called \textit{sum-product estimates}.

nodes.name: Solymosi sum-product estimate over the reals
nodes.statement: Over $\mathbb{R}$ the best-known result is due to Solymosi \cite{solymosi1}, who obtained $\max\left\{|A+A|,|A\cdot A|\right\}\gtrsim |A|^{4/3}.$

nodes.name: Rudnev sum-product estimate over $\mathbb{F}_p$
nodes.statement: The best known bound over $\mathbb{F}_p$, due to Rudnev \cite{rudnev}, is $|A|^{12/11}$ so long as $|A|<\sqrt{p}$.

nodes.name: Solymosi sum-product estimate via Szemerédi-Trotter
nodes.statement: For example the Szemer\'edi-Trotter theorem was used to establish the previously best-known sum-product result over $\mathbb{R}$ of $\max\left\{|A+A|,|A\cdot A|\right\}\gtrsim |A|^{14/11}.$

nodes.name: Improved incidence bound over $\mathbb{F}_p$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbb{F}_p$ be the finite field of prime order $p$. Let $P$ be a set of points and $L$ a set of lines in $\mathbb{F}_p^2$ with $|P|,|L|\leq N$ and $N<p$. Then $I(P,L)\ll N^{\frac{3}{2}-\frac{1}{806}+o(1)}$.
assumptions: $\mathbb{F}_p$ be the finite field of prime order $p$
$P$ be a set of points and $L$ a set of lines in $\mathbb{F}_p^2$ with $|P|,|L|\leq N$ and $N<p$
nodes.statement_short: Over $\mathbb{F}_p$ with $N<p$, $N$ points and $N$ lines have at most $N^{3/2-1/806+o(1)}$ incidences.
nodes.label: theorem:result

nodes.name: Sum-product estimates used as a black box
nodes.statement: As will be seen, the proof of Theorem \ref{theorem:result} uses finite field sum-product estimates as a `black box'. It is likely that further improvements can be obtained by unpacking the sum-product proof and exploiting its use of multiplicative energy and covering arguments to bypass some costly Balog-Szemer\'edi-Gowers type refinements.
nodes.statement_short: The proof uses sum-product bounds as a black box; unpacking them could improve the exponent.

nodes.name: Extension to general finite fields $\mathbb{F}_q$
nodes.statement: It should also be remarked that by combining recent sum-product work of Li and Roche-Newton \cite{LRN} with the approach in \cite{me1}, the exponent in Theorem \ref{theorem:result} extends to a general finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$, subject to appropriate non-degeneracy conditions. This is omitted in the interests of simplicity and instead left as an exercise for the motivated reader.
assumptions: by combining recent sum-product work of Li and Roche-Newton \cite{LRN} with the approach in \cite{me1}
conclusions: the exponent in Theorem \ref{theorem:result} extends to a general finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$
nodes.statement_short: The exponent of Theorem 3 extends to $\mathbb{F}_q$ under non-degeneracy conditions (left as an exercise).

nodes.name: Rudnev difference-ratio estimate
nodes.statement: Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$ with $|A|<\sqrt{p}$. Then $\max\left\{|A-A|,|A/ A|\right\}\gg |A|^{12/11}$.
nodes.label: theorem:rudnev

nodes.name: Geometric interpretation of Rudnev's estimate
nodes.statement: A point-set in $\mathbb{F}_p^2$ that is efficiently contained in a direct product $A \times B$ with $|A|\approx |B|<\sqrt{p}$ cannot be simultaneously covered by only a few lines through a fixed point and only a few lines with a fixed (non-vertical or horizontal) gradient. Here `few' means less than $|A|^{1+\delta}$ for a small $\delta>0$.
nodes.statement_short: A set efficiently inside $A\times B$ cannot be covered by few lines through a point and few lines of a fixed gradient.

nodes.name: Sketch of the proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: The proof of Theorem \ref{theorem:result} begins by supposing for a contradiction that $I(P,L)$ is large. By averaging arguments we can find four points $p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4 \in P$ and a large subset $R$ of $P$ that is supported on only a few lines through each of the four $p_i$. Moreover, the points $p_1,p_2,p_3$ are colinear, and the point $p_4$ lies off their common line. Apply a projective transformation $\tau$ so that lines through $\tau(p_1)$ and $\tau(p_2)$ are parallel to the vertical and horizontal co-ordinate axes respectively. This means that the image $\tau(R)$ is efficiently contained in a direct product $A \times B$. Since $\tau$ sends $p_1$ and $p_2$ to the line at infinity, and $p_3$ is colinear with both, $\tau$ must also send $p_3$ to the line at infinity. All lines passing through $\tau(p_3)$ are then parallel, but not parallel to either co-ordinate axis. So $\tau(R)$ is covered by only a few lines, all of some fixed gradient. Finally, since $p_4$ is not colinear with the other three points, $\tau(p_4)$ is not on the line at infinity. So $\tau(R)$ is covered by only a few lines, all through some fixed point. But $\tau(R)$ then satisfies the conditions that were explicitly banned in the interpretation of Lemma \ref{theorem:rudnev}, and so we obtain a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction via a projective transformation: a large set covered by few lines through four points maps into $A\times B$ violating the interpretation of Rudnev's lemma.

nodes.name: Find four points and a rich set $R$
nodes.statement: The proof of Theorem \ref{theorem:result} begins by supposing for a contradiction that $I(P,L)$ is large. By averaging arguments we can find four points $p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4 \in P$ and a large subset $R$ of $P$ that is supported on only a few lines through each of the four $p_i$. Moreover, the points $p_1,p_2,p_3$ are colinear, and the point $p_4$ lies off their common line.
nodes.statement_short: Assume many incidences; averaging gives $p_1,\dots,p_4$ and $R$ on few lines through each.

nodes.name: Projective transformation
nodes.statement: Apply a projective transformation $\tau$ so that lines through $\tau(p_1)$ and $\tau(p_2)$ are parallel to the vertical and horizontal co-ordinate axes respectively. This means that the image $\tau(R)$ is efficiently contained in a direct product $A \times B$.
nodes.statement_short: Send $p_1,p_2$ to infinity so $\tau(R)$ sits in a product set.

nodes.name: Lines of fixed gradient
nodes.statement: Since $\tau$ sends $p_1$ and $p_2$ to the line at infinity, and $p_3$ is colinear with both, $\tau$ must also send $p_3$ to the line at infinity. All lines passing through $\tau(p_3)$ are then parallel, but not parallel to either co-ordinate axis. So $\tau(R)$ is covered by only a few lines, all of some fixed gradient.
nodes.statement_short: $p_3$ goes to infinity, so $\tau(R)$ is covered by few parallel lines.

nodes.name: Lines through a fixed point
nodes.statement: Finally, since $p_4$ is not colinear with the other three points, $\tau(p_4)$ is not on the line at infinity. So $\tau(R)$ is covered by only a few lines, all through some fixed point.
nodes.statement_short: $\tau(p_4)$ is affine, so $\tau(R)$ is covered by few lines through a point.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: But $\tau(R)$ then satisfies the conditions that were explicitly banned in the interpretation of Lemma \ref{theorem:rudnev}, and so we obtain a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: This contradicts the interpretation of Rudnev's lemma.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3: setup and regularisation
nodes.statement: Suppose that $I(P,L)\gg N^{3/2-\epsilon}$. We shall show that $\epsilon\geq \frac{1}{806}-o(1)$. Without loss of generality we may assume that every point in $P$ is incident to only $O(N^{1/2+\epsilon})$ lines in $L$ and every line in $L$ is incident to only $O(N^{1/2+\epsilon})$ points in $P$. Indeed, if $P_+$ is the set of points incident to at least $C N^{1/2+\epsilon}$ lines then, writing $\delta_{pl}=1$ if $p \in l$ and $0$ otherwise, we have $$I(P_+,L)=\sum_{p \in P_+}\sum_{l \in L}\delta_{pl}\leq \frac{1}{CN^{1/2+\epsilon}}\sum_{p \in P_+}\sum_{l_1,l_2 \in L}\delta_{pl_1}\delta_{pl_2} \leq \frac{2}{C} N^{3/2+\epsilon}$$ and so $P_+$ can be discarded without affecting incidences by more than a constant. The argument for lines is similar.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $I(P,L)\gg N^{3/2-\epsilon}$; WLOG every point and line has $O(N^{1/2+\epsilon})$ incidences by discarding rich ones.

nodes.name: Assume many incidences
nodes.statement: Suppose that $I(P,L)\gg N^{3/2-\epsilon}$. We shall show that $\epsilon\geq \frac{1}{806}-o(1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $I(P,L)\gg N^{3/2-\epsilon}$ and aim to bound $\epsilon$ below.

nodes.name: Discard rich points and lines
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality we may assume that every point in $P$ is incident to only $O(N^{1/2+\epsilon})$ lines in $L$ and every line in $L$ is incident to only $O(N^{1/2+\epsilon})$ points in $P$. Indeed, if $P_+$ is the set of points incident to at least $C N^{1/2+\epsilon}$ lines then, writing $\delta_{pl}=1$ if $p \in l$ and $0$ otherwise, we have $$I(P_+,L)=\sum_{p \in P_+}\sum_{l \in L}\delta_{pl}\leq \frac{1}{CN^{1/2+\epsilon}}\sum_{p \in P_+}\sum_{l_1,l_2 \in L}\delta_{pl_1}\delta_{pl_2} \leq \frac{2}{C} N^{3/2+\epsilon}$$ and so $P_+$ can be discarded without affecting incidences by more than a constant. The argument for lines is similar.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG bounded degrees: rich points carry few incidences by double counting.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3: plan of the partial sum-product step
nodes.statement: Our first aim is to show that if $\epsilon$ is small then there must exist large $A,B \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$ and a large $E \subseteq A \times B$ such that $A\stackrel{E}{-}B$ and $A\stackrel{E}{/}B$ are both small. This is accomplished by making two iterations of a refinement argument, and then applying a projective transformation.
nodes.statement_short: Plan: two refinements and a projective map produce $E\subseteq A\times B$ with small partial difference and ratio sets.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3: first refinement
nodes.statement: Let $P_1$ be the set of points in $P$ incident to $\Omega\left(N^{1/2-\epsilon}\right)$ lines in $L$. By a dyadic pigeonholing we may find a subset $P_1'\subseteq P_1$ and an integer $K$ with $$N^{1/2- \epsilon}\ll K \ll N^{1/2+\epsilon}$$ such that every point in $P_1'$ is incident to between $K$ and $2K$ lines in $L$, and $I(P_1',L)\approx|P_1'|K \approx N^{3/2-\epsilon}$. Now let $L_1$ be the set of lines in $L$ incident to $\widetilde{\Omega}\left(N^{1/2-\epsilon}\right)$ points in $P_1'$, and $P_2$ be the set of points in $P_1'$ incident to $\widetilde{\Omega}\left(K\right)$ lines in $L_1$. Note that $I(P_2,L_1)\approx I(P_1',L_1)\approx I(P_1',L)\approx N^{3/2-\epsilon}$ because in each case we can pick constants to ensure that only a fraction of the $N^{3/2-\epsilon}$ incidences are discarded. Note also that $|P_2|\gtrsim N^{1-2\epsilon}$ and in particular that $P_2$ has at least say 100 elements. For each $p \in P_2$ let $P_p=\left\{q \in P_1':l_{pq}\in L_1\right\}$. Since $p$ is incident to $\widetilde{\Omega}(K)$ lines in $L_1$ and each line is incident to at least $\widetilde{\Omega}(N^{1/2-\epsilon})$ points in $P_1'$ we have $|P_p|\gtrsim K N^{1/2-\epsilon}$. Summing over all such $p$ and applying Cauchy-Schwartz gives \begin{equation} K N^{1/2-\epsilon}|P_2|\lesssim \sum_{p \in P_2}|P_2| \leq |P_1|^{1/2}\left(\sum_{p_1,p_2}\left|P_{p_1}\cap P_{p_2}\right|\right)^{1/2} \end{equation} and so $$\frac{K^2 |P_2|^2}{N^{2\epsilon}} \lesssim \sum_{p_1,p_2 \in P_2}\left|P_{p_1}\cap P_{p_2}\right|$$ Now, $\sum_{p \in P_2}|P_p| \leq |P_2|N$, and this is certainly far less that $\frac{K^2 |P_2|^2}{N^{2\epsilon}}$ or we are already done. So we may assume that the summation on the right is over distinct pairs $p_1,p_2$. There then exist distinct $p_1,p_2$ with $\left|P_{p_1}\cap P_{p_2}\right|\gtrsim K^2/N^{2 \epsilon}$.
nodes.statement_short: Dyadic pigeonholing then Cauchy-Schwarz. Finds distinct $p_1,p_2$ with $|P_{p_1}\cap P_{p_2}|\gtrsim K^2/N^{2\epsilon}$.

nodes.name: Dyadic pigeonholing
nodes.statement: Let $P_1$ be the set of points in $P$ incident to $\Omega\left(N^{1/2-\epsilon}\right)$ lines in $L$. By a dyadic pigeonholing we may find a subset $P_1'\subseteq P_1$ and an integer $K$ with $$N^{1/2- \epsilon}\ll K \ll N^{1/2+\epsilon}$$ such that every point in $P_1'$ is incident to between $K$ and $2K$ lines in $L$, and $I(P_1',L)\approx|P_1'|K \approx N^{3/2-\epsilon}$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $P_1$ and pigeonhole to $P_1'$ with degrees in $[K,2K]$.

nodes.name: Rich lines and points
nodes.statement: Now let $L_1$ be the set of lines in $L$ incident to $\widetilde{\Omega}\left(N^{1/2-\epsilon}\right)$ points in $P_1'$, and $P_2$ be the set of points in $P_1'$ incident to $\widetilde{\Omega}\left(K\right)$ lines in $L_1$. Note that $I(P_2,L_1)\approx I(P_1',L_1)\approx I(P_1',L)\approx N^{3/2-\epsilon}$ because in each case we can pick constants to ensure that only a fraction of the $N^{3/2-\epsilon}$ incidences are discarded. Note also that $|P_2|\gtrsim N^{1-2\epsilon}$ and in particular that $P_2$ has at least say 100 elements.
nodes.statement_short: Define $L_1$ and $P_2$, which retain most incidences.

nodes.name: Define $P_p$
nodes.statement: For each $p \in P_2$ let $P_p=\left\{q \in P_1':l_{pq}\in L_1\right\}$. Since $p$ is incident to $\widetilde{\Omega}(K)$ lines in $L_1$ and each line is incident to at least $\widetilde{\Omega}(N^{1/2-\epsilon})$ points in $P_1'$ we have $|P_p|\gtrsim K N^{1/2-\epsilon}$.
nodes.statement_short: Each $P_p$ has size $\gtrsim KN^{1/2-\epsilon}$.

nodes.name: Cauchy-Schwarz
nodes.statement: Summing over all such $p$ and applying Cauchy-Schwartz gives \begin{equation} K N^{1/2-\epsilon}|P_2|\lesssim \sum_{p \in P_2}|P_2| \leq |P_1|^{1/2}\left(\sum_{p_1,p_2}\left|P_{p_1}\cap P_{p_2}\right|\right)^{1/2} \end{equation} and so $$\frac{K^2 |P_2|^2}{N^{2\epsilon}} \lesssim \sum_{p_1,p_2 \in P_2}\left|P_{p_1}\cap P_{p_2}\right|$$ Now, $\sum_{p \in P_2}|P_p| \leq |P_2|N$, and this is certainly far less that $\frac{K^2 |P_2|^2}{N^{2\epsilon}}$ or we are already done.
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz lower-bounds the sum of $|P_{p_1}\cap P_{p_2}|$.

nodes.name: Find $p_1,p_2$
nodes.statement: So we may assume that the summation on the right is over distinct pairs $p_1,p_2$. There then exist distinct $p_1,p_2$ with $\left|P_{p_1}\cap P_{p_2}\right|\gtrsim K^2/N^{2 \epsilon}$.
nodes.statement_short: Some distinct pair $p_1,p_2$ has a large common set.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3: second refinement
nodes.statement: Define $Q=P_{p_1}\cap P_{p_2}$, so that (passing to a subset if necessary) $$|Q|\approx K^2/N^{2\epsilon}$$ and $$I(Q,L)\approx K^3/N^{2\epsilon}.$$ Moreover, note that $Q$ is supported over only $O(K)$ lines through each of $p_1$ and $p_2$. We now build a similar argument for the set $Q$. We let $J$ be the set of lines in $L$ incident to $\widetilde{\Omega}\left(K^3/N^{1+2\epsilon}\right)$ points in $Q$, and $Q_1$ be the set of points in $Q$ incident to $\widetilde{\Omega}\left(K\right)$ lines in $J$. Note that $I(Q_1,J)\approx I(Q,J)\approx I(Q,L)\approx K^3/N^{2\epsilon}$. Points in $Q_1$ are supported over $O(K)$ lines through $p_1$, each incident to $O(N^{1/2+\epsilon})$ points, and we also know $|Q_1|\gtrsim N^{1-6 \epsilon}$. So there are several (in fact $\widetilde{\Omega}(N^{1/2-7\epsilon})$) lines in $J$ that are each incident to $p_1$ and also $\widetilde{\Omega}(N^{1/2-7\epsilon})$ points in $Q$. Pick one such line that is not incident to $p_2$. Let $Q_2$ be the set of points from $Q_1$ on that line. For each $p \in Q_2$ let $Q_p=\left\{q \in Q:l_{pq}\in J\right\}$, so that $|Q_p|\gtrsim K^4/N^{1+2 \epsilon}$. We have $$\frac{K^4}{N^{1+2\epsilon}}|Q_2|\lesssim \sum_{p \in Q_2}|Q_p|$$ and so applying Cauchy Schwartz as in (\ref{eq:CS}) we find distinct $p_3,p_4 \in Q_2$, not equal to $p_1,p_2$, such that $|Q_{p_3}\cap Q_{p_4}|\gtrsim \frac{K^8}{N^{2+4\epsilon}|Q|}\approx \frac{K^6}{N^{2+2\epsilon}}$. Define $R= Q_{p_3}\cap Q_{p_4}$ so that $$|R|\gtrsim K^6/N^{2+2 \epsilon}$$ and $R$ is supported on $O(K)$ lines through each of $p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4$.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat the refinement on $Q$ along a line through $p_1$. Yields $p_3,p_4$ and a set $R$ on $O(K)$ lines through each $p_i$.

nodes.name: Define $Q$
nodes.statement: Define $Q=P_{p_1}\cap P_{p_2}$, so that (passing to a subset if necessary) $$|Q|\approx K^2/N^{2\epsilon}$$ and $$I(Q,L)\approx K^3/N^{2\epsilon}.$$ Moreover, note that $Q$ is supported over only $O(K)$ lines through each of $p_1$ and $p_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Set $Q=P_{p_1}\cap P_{p_2}$ with its size and incidence count.

nodes.name: Rich lines $J$ and points $Q_1$
nodes.statement: We now build a similar argument for the set $Q$. We let $J$ be the set of lines in $L$ incident to $\widetilde{\Omega}\left(K^3/N^{1+2\epsilon}\right)$ points in $Q$, and $Q_1$ be the set of points in $Q$ incident to $\widetilde{\Omega}\left(K\right)$ lines in $J$. Note that $I(Q_1,J)\approx I(Q,J)\approx I(Q,L)\approx K^3/N^{2\epsilon}$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $J$ and $Q_1$ retaining most incidences of $Q$.

nodes.name: Choose a line through $p_1$
nodes.statement: Points in $Q_1$ are supported over $O(K)$ lines through $p_1$, each incident to $O(N^{1/2+\epsilon})$ points, and we also know $|Q_1|\gtrsim N^{1-6 \epsilon}$. So there are several (in fact $\widetilde{\Omega}(N^{1/2-7\epsilon})$) lines in $J$ that are each incident to $p_1$ and also $\widetilde{\Omega}(N^{1/2-7\epsilon})$ points in $Q$. Pick one such line that is not incident to $p_2$. Let $Q_2$ be the set of points from $Q_1$ on that line.
nodes.statement_short: A rich line through $p_1$, not through $p_2$, gives $Q_2$.

nodes.name: Cauchy-Schwarz again
nodes.statement: For each $p \in Q_2$ let $Q_p=\left\{q \in Q:l_{pq}\in J\right\}$, so that $|Q_p|\gtrsim K^4/N^{1+2 \epsilon}$. We have $$\frac{K^4}{N^{1+2\epsilon}}|Q_2|\lesssim \sum_{p \in Q_2}|Q_p|$$ and so applying Cauchy Schwartz as in (\ref{eq:CS}) we find distinct $p_3,p_4 \in Q_2$, not equal to $p_1,p_2$, such that $|Q_{p_3}\cap Q_{p_4}|\gtrsim \frac{K^8}{N^{2+4\epsilon}|Q|}\approx \frac{K^6}{N^{2+2\epsilon}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz as in (1) gives $p_3,p_4$ with large $|Q_{p_3}\cap Q_{p_4}|$.

nodes.name: Define $R$
nodes.statement: Define $R= Q_{p_3}\cap Q_{p_4}$ so that $$|R|\gtrsim K^6/N^{2+2 \epsilon}$$ and $R$ is supported on $O(K)$ lines through each of $p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4$.
nodes.statement_short: $R$ is large and on $O(K)$ lines through each $p_i$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3: projective transformation
nodes.statement: Since $p_3,p_4 \in Q_2$ they are colinear with $p_1$ but not $p_2$. Pick a projective transformation $\tau$ that sends their common line to the line at infinity, in such a way that lines through $p_3$ and $p_4$ are parallel to the horiztonal and vertical co-ordinate axes respectively. If we define $E=\tau(R)$ then this means that $E \subseteq A \times B$ for $A,B \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$. By appending points if neccesary we may assume $$|A|,|B| \approx K.$$ And by discarding points we may assume that $$|E|\approx K^6/N^{2+2 \epsilon}.$$ Since $p_1$ is colinear with $p_3$ and $p_4$, lines through $\tau(p_1)$ are all parallel, but not parallel to the vertical or horizontal axes. So there exists $z \notin \left\{0,\infty\right\}$ such that $E$ is supported on only $O(K)$ lines of gradient $z$. Since $p_2$ is not colinear with $p_3$, the map $\tau$ sends it to the affine plane, and so $E$ is supported on $O(K)$ lines all passing through $\tau(p_2)$. Note that these properties are invariant under translation of the plane and scaling of a single co-ordinate axis in the following sense. First, if $T$ is some translation of the plane then $T(E)$ is supported on $O(K)$ lines through $T(\tau(p_2))$, and still covered by $O(K)$ lines of gradient $z$. So we may assume that $\tau(p_2)$ is the origin. Second, if $\delta_{\lambda}$ is the transformation that sends $(x,y)$ to $(x,\lambda y)$, then $(x,y)$ lies on the line $y=mx+c$ if and only if $\delta_{\lambda}(x,y)$ lies on the line $y=(\lambda m) x+ \lambda c$. So $\delta_{\lambda}(E)$ is supported on $O(K)$ lines of gradient $\lambda z$ and $O(K)$ lines through the origin. By taking $\lambda = 1/z$ we may assume therefore that $z=1$. So without loss of generality we may assume that $E$ is supported on $O(K)$ lines through the origin and $O(K)$ lines of gradient 1. In other words $$\left|A \stackrel{E}{/}B\right|,\left|A \stackrel{E}{-}B\right|\ll K.$$
nodes.statement_short: Projective map sending the line $p_1p_3p_4$ to infinity, then translate and rescale. Gives $|A\stackrel{E}{/}B|,|A\stackrel{E}{-}B|\ll K$.

nodes.name: Projective transformation $\tau$
nodes.statement: Since $p_3,p_4 \in Q_2$ they are colinear with $p_1$ but not $p_2$. Pick a projective transformation $\tau$ that sends their common line to the line at infinity, in such a way that lines through $p_3$ and $p_4$ are parallel to the horiztonal and vertical co-ordinate axes respectively. If we define $E=\tau(R)$ then this means that $E \subseteq A \times B$ for $A,B \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$. By appending points if neccesary we may assume $$|A|,|B| \approx K.$$ And by discarding points we may assume that $$|E|\approx K^6/N^{2+2 \epsilon}.$$

nodes.name: Lines of fixed gradient
nodes.statement: Since $p_1$ is colinear with $p_3$ and $p_4$, lines through $\tau(p_1)$ are all parallel, but not parallel to the vertical or horizontal axes. So there exists $z \notin \left\{0,\infty\right\}$ such that $E$ is supported on only $O(K)$ lines of gradient $z$.
nodes.statement_short: $E$ lies on $O(K)$ lines of a gradient $z\ne 0,\infty$.

nodes.name: Lines through a point
nodes.statement: Since $p_2$ is not colinear with $p_3$, the map $\tau$ sends it to the affine plane, and so $E$ is supported on $O(K)$ lines all passing through $\tau(p_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: $E$ lies on $O(K)$ lines through $\tau(p_2)$.

nodes.name: Translate
nodes.statement: Note that these properties are invariant under translation of the plane and scaling of a single co-ordinate axis in the following sense. First, if $T$ is some translation of the plane then $T(E)$ is supported on $O(K)$ lines through $T(\tau(p_2))$, and still covered by $O(K)$ lines of gradient $z$. So we may assume that $\tau(p_2)$ is the origin.
nodes.statement_short: Translate so $\tau(p_2)$ is the origin.

nodes.name: Rescale
nodes.statement: Second, if $\delta_{\lambda}$ is the transformation that sends $(x,y)$ to $(x,\lambda y)$, then $(x,y)$ lies on the line $y=mx+c$ if and only if $\delta_{\lambda}(x,y)$ lies on the line $y=(\lambda m) x+ \lambda c$. So $\delta_{\lambda}(E)$ is supported on $O(K)$ lines of gradient $\lambda z$ and $O(K)$ lines through the origin. By taking $\lambda = 1/z$ we may assume therefore that $z=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Rescale one axis so that $z=1$.

nodes.name: Small partial difference and ratio sets
nodes.statement: So without loss of generality we may assume that $E$ is supported on $O(K)$ lines through the origin and $O(K)$ lines of gradient 1. In other words $$\left|A \stackrel{E}{/}B\right|,\left|A \stackrel{E}{-}B\right|\ll K.$$
nodes.statement_short: Hence partial difference and ratio sets are $\ll K$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3: conclusion
nodes.statement: We want to apply sum-product (or strictly speaking, difference-ratio) estimates to the \textit{partial} difference and ratio sets that we have just constructed. To do this we need to work with \textit{complete} difference and ratio sets. The traditional machinery for making such a transition is the Balog-Szemer\'edi-Gowers theorem. We employ a variation, itself a straightforward modification of one due to Bourgain and Garaev \cite{bg}: \begin{lemma} Let $A,B \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$ and $E \subseteq A \times B$. Then there exists $A' \subseteq A$ with $|A'|\gg \frac{|E|}{|B|}$ and $\frac{|A'-A'|}{\left|A\stackrel{E}{-}B\right|^4},\frac{|(A'/A'|}{\left|A\stackrel{E}{/}B\right|^4}\ll \frac{|A|^4|B|^3}{|E|^5}$. \end{lemma} A proof of Lemma \ref{theorem:bg} is given in the appendix. To apply Lemma \ref{theorem:bg} we note that since $K\gg N^{1/2-\epsilon}$ we have $$\frac{|E|}{|B|}\approx \frac{K^5}{N^{2+2 \epsilon}}\gg N^{1/2-7 \epsilon}$$ and $$\frac{|A|^4|B|^3\left|A\stackrel{E}{-}B\right|^4}{|E|^5}, \frac{|A|^4|B|^3\left|A\stackrel{E}{/}B\right|^4}{|E|^5} \ll \frac{N^{10+10\epsilon}}{K^{19}} \ll N^{1/2+29 \epsilon}.$$ So there exists $A' \subseteq A$ with $|A'|\gtrsim N^{1/2-7 \epsilon}$ and $|A'-A'|,|A'/A'|\lesssim N^{1/2+29\epsilon}$. Applying Lemma \ref{theorem:rudnev} to $A'$ yields $N^{1/2}\lesssim N^{403 \epsilon}$ and so $\epsilon \geq \frac{1}{806}-o(1)$, which completes the proof of Theorem \ref{theorem:result}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Balog-Szemerédi-Gowers variant (Lemma 5) then Rudnev's estimate. Exponent count gives $\epsilon\ge 1/806-o(1)$.

nodes.name: Balog-Szemerédi-Gowers variant
nodes.statement: We want to apply sum-product (or strictly speaking, difference-ratio) estimates to the \textit{partial} difference and ratio sets that we have just constructed. To do this we need to work with \textit{complete} difference and ratio sets. The traditional machinery for making such a transition is the Balog-Szemer\'edi-Gowers theorem. We employ a variation, itself a straightforward modification of one due to Bourgain and Garaev \cite{bg}: \begin{lemma} Let $A,B \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$ and $E \subseteq A \times B$. Then there exists $A' \subseteq A$ with $|A'|\gg \frac{|E|}{|B|}$ and $\frac{|A'-A'|}{\left|A\stackrel{E}{-}B\right|^4},\frac{|(A'/A'|}{\left|A\stackrel{E}{/}B\right|^4}\ll \frac{|A|^4|B|^3}{|E|^5}$. \end{lemma} A proof of Lemma \ref{theorem:bg} is given in the appendix.
nodes.statement_short: State Lemma 5 to pass from partial to complete difference and ratio sets.

nodes.name: Check hypotheses of Lemma 5

nodes.statement_short: Bound the quantities in Lemma 5 in terms of $N$ and $\epsilon$.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 5
nodes.statement: So there exists $A' \subseteq A$ with $|A'|\gtrsim N^{1/2-7 \epsilon}$ and $|A'-A'|,|A'/A'|\lesssim N^{1/2+29\epsilon}$.
nodes.statement_short: Get $A'$ with small $A'-A'$ and $A'/A'$.

nodes.name: Apply Rudnev's lemma
nodes.statement: Applying Lemma \ref{theorem:rudnev} to $A'$ yields $N^{1/2}\lesssim N^{403 \epsilon}$ and so $\epsilon \geq \frac{1}{806}-o(1)$, which completes the proof of Theorem \ref{theorem:result}.
nodes.statement_short: Rudnev's lemma forces $\epsilon\ge 1/806-o(1)$.

nodes.name: Cauchy-Schwarz bound for $P_2$
nodes.statement: K N^{1/2-\epsilon}|P_2|\lesssim \sum_{p \in P_2}|P_2| \leq |P_1|^{1/2}\left(\sum_{p_1,p_2}\left|P_{p_1}\cap P_{p_2}\right|\right)^{1/2}
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz bound relating $|P_2|$ to pairwise intersections $|P_{p_1}\cap P_{p_2}|$.
nodes.label: eq:CS

nodes.name: Bourgain-Garaev type Balog-Szemerédi-Gowers lemma
nodes.statement: Let $A,B \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$ and $E \subseteq A \times B$. Then there exists $A' \subseteq A$ with $|A'|\gg \frac{|E|}{|B|}$ and $\frac{|A'-A'|}{\left|A\stackrel{E}{-}B\right|^4},\frac{|(A'/A'|}{\left|A\stackrel{E}{/}B\right|^4}\ll \frac{|A|^4|B|^3}{|E|^5}$.
nodes.statement_short: Large $A'\subseteq A$ whose full difference and ratio sets are controlled by partial ones along $E$.
nodes.label: theorem:bg

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5
nodes.statement: The proof of Lemma \ref{theorem:bg} follows the approach in \cite{bg} closely, making only a slight technical modification. The following lemma can be found in the book of Tao and Vu \cite{TV}: \begin{lemma} Let $E \subseteq A \times B$. Then for any $\epsilon >0$ there exists $A' \subseteq A$ with $|A'|\gg \frac{|E|}{|B|} $ such that for at least $(1-\epsilon)|A'|^2$ of the pairs $(a_1',a_2') \in A'\times A'$ we have $$\left|N(a_1')\cap N(a_2')\right|\geq \frac{\epsilon |E|^2}{2|A|^2|B|}$$ where $N(a)$ is the set of $b\in B$ for which $(a,b) \in E$. \end{lemma} We apply it to obtain: \begin{lemma} Let $G(A,B,E)$ be a bipartite graph. Then there exists $A'\subseteq A$ with $|A'|\gg \frac{|E|}{|B|}$ such that every pair of elements from $A' \times A'$ is connected by $\Omega\left(\frac{|E|^5}{|A|^4|B|^3}\right)$ paths of length four in $E$. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Say that $(a_1,a_2)\in A \times A$ is \textbf{good} if $$\left|N(a_1)\cap N(a_2)\right|\geq 0.05 \frac{|E|^2}{|A|^2|B|}.$$ By the previous lemma we can find $|A'|\gg \frac{|E|}{|B|}$ such that $0.9 |A'|^2$ of pairs from $A'$ are good. Given $a_1'\in A'$ denote by $I_{a_1'}$ the set of elements $a_2' \in A'$ for which $(a_1',a_2')$ is good. Then we have $$\sum_{a' \in A'}|I_{a'}|\geq 0.9 |A'|^2.$$ So by popularity pigeonholing there exists $|A''|\gg|A'|$ such that $|I_a|\geq 0.7|A'| $ for every $a \in A''$. So for any pair $a_1,a_2 \in A''$ we have $|I_{a_1}\cap I_{a_2}|\gg |A'|$ and so there are $\Omega(|A'|)$ elements $c \in A'$ for which $$|N(a_1)\cap N(c)|,|N(a_2)\cap N(c)|\gg \frac{|E|^2}{|A|^2|B|}.$$ This means that there are $\Omega \left(\frac{|E|^5}{|A|^4|B|^3}\right)$ paths of length four in $E$ connecting $a_1$ and $a_2$, as required. \end{proof} To prove Lemma \ref{theorem:bg} we note that for each $\alpha,\beta \in A'$ we have, $$\#\left\{(b_1,a,b_2)\in B \times A \times B:(\alpha,b_1),(a,b_1),(a_1,b_2),(\beta,b_2)\in E\right\}\gg \frac{|E|^5}{|A|^4|B|^3}.$$ Now it is clear that \begin{align*} \alpha-\beta&= (\alpha-b_1)-(c-b_1)+(a-b_2)-(\beta-b_2)\\ \frac{\alpha}{\beta}&=\frac{\alpha}{b_1}\cdot \frac{b_1}{a} \cdot \frac{a}{b_2}\cdot \frac{b_2}{\beta}. \end{align*} So for all $\alpha,\beta \in A'$ we have $$\#\left\{(s,t,u,v)\in A\stackrel{E}{-}B:s-t+u-v=\alpha-\beta\right\}\gg\frac{|E|^5}{|A|^4|B|^3} $$ $$\#\left\{(s,t,u,v)\in A\stackrel{E}{\backslash}B:\frac{st}{uv}=\frac{\alpha}{\beta}\right\}\gg \frac{|E|^5}{|A|^4|B|^3}.$$ Summing over all elements of $A'-A'$ and $A'/A'$ respectively, we obtain $$\frac{|E|^5}{|A|^4|B|^3}|A'-A'|\ll\left|A \stackrel{E}{-}B \right|^4 $$ $$\frac{|E|^5}{|A|^4|B|^3}|A'/A'|\ll\left|A \stackrel{E}{/}B\right|^4. $$ Rearranging gives the statment of Lemma \ref{theorem:bg}.
nodes.statement_short: Paths of length four (Lemma 7) give many representations of $\alpha-\beta$ and $\alpha/\beta$. Counting them bounds $|A'-A'|$ and $|A'/A'|$.

nodes.name: Auxiliary lemmas

Then there exists $A'\subseteq A$ with $|A'|\gg \frac{|E|}{|B|}$ such that every pair of elements from $A' \times A'$ is connected by $\Omega\left(\frac{|E|^5}{|A|^4|B|^3}\right)$ paths of length four in $E$. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Say that $(a_1,a_2)\in A \times A$ is \textbf{good} if $$\left|N(a_1)\cap N(a_2)\right|\geq 0.05 \frac{|E|^2}{|A|^2|B|}.$$ By the previous lemma we can find $|A'|\gg \frac{|E|}{|B|}$ such that $0.9 |A'|^2$ of pairs from $A'$ are good. nodes.name: Count paths
nodes.statement: To prove Lemma \ref{theorem:bg} we note that for each $\alpha,\beta \in A'$ we have, $$\#\left\{(b_1,a,b_2)\in B \times A \times B:(\alpha,b_1),(a,b_1),(a_1,b_2),(\beta,b_2)\in E\right\}\gg \frac{|E|^5}{|A|^4|B|^3}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 7 gives many paths between any $\alpha,\beta\in A'$.

nodes.name: Telescoping identities
nodes.statement: Now it is clear that \begin{align*} \alpha-\beta&= (\alpha-b_1)-(c-b_1)+(a-b_2)-(\beta-b_2)\\ \frac{\alpha}{\beta}&=\frac{\alpha}{b_1}\cdot \frac{b_1}{a} \cdot \frac{a}{b_2}\cdot \frac{b_2}{\beta}. \end{align*} So for all $\alpha,\beta \in A'$ we have $$\#\left\{(s,t,u,v)\in A\stackrel{E}{-}B:s-t+u-v=\alpha-\beta\right\}\gg\frac{|E|^5}{|A|^4|B|^3} $$ $$\#\left\{(s,t,u,v)\in A\stackrel{E}{\backslash}B:\frac{st}{uv}=\frac{\alpha}{\beta}\right\}\gg \frac{|E|^5}{|A|^4|B|^3}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Each path represents $\alpha-\beta$ and $\alpha/\beta$ via partial differences and ratios.

nodes.name: Sum and rearrange
nodes.statement: Summing over all elements of $A'-A'$ and $A'/A'$ respectively, we obtain $$\frac{|E|^5}{|A|^4|B|^3}|A'-A'|\ll\left|A \stackrel{E}{-}B \right|^4 $$ $$\frac{|E|^5}{|A|^4|B|^3}|A'/A'|\ll\left|A \stackrel{E}{/}B\right|^4. $$ Rearranging gives the statment of Lemma \ref{theorem:bg}.
nodes.statement_short: Summing over $A'-A'$ and $A'/A'$ gives the lemma.

nodes.name: Tao-Vu popular pairs lemma
nodes.statement: Let $E \subseteq A \times B$. Then for any $\epsilon >0$ there exists $A' \subseteq A$ with $|A'|\gg \frac{|E|}{|B|} $ such that for at least $(1-\epsilon)|A'|^2$ of the pairs $(a_1',a_2') \in A'\times A'$ we have $$\left|N(a_1')\cap N(a_2')\right|\geq \frac{\epsilon |E|^2}{2|A|^2|B|}$$ where $N(a)$ is the set of $b\in B$ for which $(a,b) \in E$.
